Teaching counterexample‘The authorization was invalid, so the statement and its effects never existed.’

What it limitsJudgments of authority cannot erase demonstrable actions, consequences, and repair responsibilities.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexamplePassing the “validity of the delegation” branch automatically expands the scope of authorization within the same record.

What it limitsThe first three branches cannot change the scope of authorization; authority transfer requires the separate “transfer of authority” branch and its simultaneous conditions.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • This lesson makes no unverified determination of any real individual's authorization validity; historical action records are not complete legal-authorization files.
  • Withdrawal or expiration must be handled according to authorization conditions; past validity does not guarantee present validity.
  • Repair must not erase existing actions and consequences, or use consequences already caused to manufacture authority retroactively.

Scope and open questions

Historical accounts of action help distinguish actual participation from representative standing unsupported by evidence; missing authorization evidence is not treated as invalid authorization.

Self-appointed claims, actual acts on others' behalf, and demonstrable effects may still be recorded; expansion of the scope of authorization cannot be determined on that basis.

If A may report on project A and B may sign for receipt for project B, does that imply A may sign for receipt for project B?

No. Authorization consists of complete pairings; its items cannot be split and cross-combined.

Does passing the valid-delegation branch already complete a transfer of authority within the scope of authorization?

Not necessarily. The source requires the transfer-of-authority branch, complete itemized authorizations, independent validity, and what this transformation states about authorization to pass together.

When authorization is found invalid, should past actions be deleted?

No. Retain facts and consequences, restrict subsequent action, and arrange responsible correction.

5.5.8Compression or Abstraction (M08) ​

In briefCompression need not impair the current task, but one must specify which answer is preserved and which distinctions are collapsed. Inability to recover the original and inability to answer the current question are different conclusions.

Compression or abstraction is summed up as “many-to-one representational compression.” The source material, algorithm, threshold, version used, error, irrecoverable information, and invariants required for the task must all be traceable. The four statuses “unknown,” “not applicable,” “unobservable,” and “withheld for protection” must be kept distinct, and none of them can be compressed into “absent.” A representation with material task-relevant losses for a proposed high-impact action must not be used to support that action.

Compression can be illustrated by a precise condition for task sufficiency. Let x be the source state, z=f(x) its representation, and q(x) the answer currently required. There exists a function g such that q=g∘f if and only if f(x₁)=f(x₂) always implies q(x₁)=q(x₂). The condition shows that the original state may be irrecoverable even when the current question can still be answered exactly. It gives no guarantee that g is easy to compute or that the representation remains sufficient for a different question, environment, or intervention. 〔Studies 05.01–05.02, 05.05–05.06, formal illustration here〕

Consider a finite, nonempty state domain and a real-valued target q. If the decoder can output any real number and loss is measured by the worst-case absolute error over the whole domain, the minimum recovery error from the representation is exactly half the largest oscillation of the target within a preimage. A preimage here means all the source states mapped to the same representation. Let a_z and b_z denote the minimum and maximum target values in each nonempty preimage. The optimal error is (1/2)max_z(b_z−a_z), attained by outputting the midpoint for each preimage. Given a tolerance ε, there exists a decoder with error at most ε if and only if the oscillation within each preimage is at most 2ε. The formula cannot be applied directly to vector or integer outputs, average loss, or an unknown distribution.

Successive conversions must preserve the same final question. Let f:X→Z and h:Z→W, and let the first stage be sufficient for the final target q, that is, q=g∘f. The final representation h∘f remains sufficient if and only if g is constant on every preimage under h restricted to the actual image f(X). Unreachable intermediate values need not be constrained. Nor can the completion of a different local task at the second stage close the original final question. See Appendix C.6–C.7 for the condition and its proof.

5.5.8Note

Understanding this section

5.5.8 Compression or abstraction (M08)

Compression need not impair the current task, but one must specify which answer is preserved and which distinctions are collapsed. Inability to recover the original and inability to answer the current question are different conclusions.

Compression or abstraction maps multiple source states to the same representation. Track source material, algorithms, thresholds, versions, errors, unrecoverable information, and task-required invariants. Keep “unknown,” “not applicable,” “unobservable” (not observable under current conditions), and “withheld for protection” distinct; none means nonexistent.

The exact condition is stated in terms of source state x, representation z=f(x), and final query q(x). If two states share a representation but require different answers, any decoder reading only z can give just one answer and cannot be correct for both. Conversely, if q is constant within every nonempty preimage, define g(z) as that common value, yielding q=g∘f. This is a proof in both directions, not merely a rule of thumb that ‘usually works.’

Here g may read only the declared representation; it cannot secretly use source-state identity, the original, or undeclared history. Existence of a set function does not imply an efficient algorithm, or guarantee sufficiency after changing the task, environment, or permitted intervention. For example, a sum can answer a total but not necessarily a maximum or which location exceeds a limit.

Approximate recovery first requires a fixed loss. Under four groups of premises—finite nonempty X, real-valued target q, arbitrary real-valued outputs, and global worst-case absolute error—take minimum a_z and maximum b_z within each nonempty preimage z. Any output c is at least (b_z−a_z)/2 from one endpoint, because the distance between endpoints is no greater than |a_z−c|+|c−b_z|. Thus every decoder's global error is at least half the largest preimage range.

Outputting midpoint (a_z+b_z)/2 for each preimage puts every target in its interval within half the range, with endpoints attaining that distance. Taking the maximum across preimages reaches the lower bound above. The optimal error is therefore exactly (1/2)max_z(b_z−a_z). For nonnegative ε, a decoder with error ≤ε exists if and only if every preimage range is ≤2ε.

This is not a universal loss score across domains. Integer outputs may exclude the midpoint; vector targets require a specified norm and geometry; average loss depends on a distribution; an unknown distribution does not allow population error rates to follow from this formula. Changed conditions require redefining and solving the optimization problem.

Successive compression must also retain the same final query. Let f:X→Z, h:Z→W, and q=g∘f. The composition can still recover q if and only if g is constant on every preimage of h restricted to the actual image f(X). Necessity: identical final representations can give only the same answer. Sufficiency: define k using the common g value in each reachable final preimage; then q=k∘h∘f. Intermediate values unreachable from any source state need not satisfy this constraint.

The first stage completing storage and the second completing counting cannot settle the original final task of ‘identifying the first position.’ Changing the task may produce another successful result, but it must be recorded separately, without overwriting failure on the old task. A representation with substantial task-relevant loss for a proposed high-impact action cannot support that action. Retaining the complete original provides a repair resource, but whether the implementer could obtain and use it in time at the relevant moment must still be checked.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Predefine the final query, object domain, representation algorithm, and available inputs; state versions and missing-data statuses.

  2. 2

    Partition source states into nonempty preimages sharing the same representation, and check whether answers agree within each.

  3. 3

    For exact recovery, prove existence using preimage constancy or give a counterexample of two conflicting states.

  4. 4

    For approximate recovery, first fix conditions such as real-valued outputs and worst-case absolute error, then calculate each preimage's range and midpoint.

  5. 5

    Keep the same q across multiple transformations, checking whether final-stage merges retain identical answers only on the actually reachable intermediate image.

  6. 6

    Separate representational sufficiency from actual algorithm correctness; prohibit covert access to undeclared source material.

  7. 7

    For high-impact uses, recheck task-relevant loss, protection, norms, and authority; usability of a low-risk summary cannot simply carry over.

Distinctions to keep clear

Recover all source states

Requires information that distinguishes every relevant x.

≠

Recover the current answer

Requires only that q be constant in each representation preimage, which can be a weaker requirement.

Function existence

The correct answer can be mathematically defined from the representation.

≠

Computable and executable in time

Also involves algorithms, budgets, input accessibility, and actual execution.

Local task success

That segment completes its own declared work.

≠

Preservation of the final query

The entire chain remains sufficient for the same q; the question cannot be changed.

Unavoidable representational error

A lower bound arising from conflicting answers within the same preimage.

≠

Additional errors from the actual rule

May be introduced by inappropriate decoding and require separate checking.

Mathematical construction: the mean answers a total but not a local extremeTeaching scenario

AssumptionsA complete two-state domain, exact values, and a deterministic mapping; the decoder reads only the mean.

Let X={(0,10),(5,5)} and f take the mean of the two numbers, giving 5 for both. If q₁ takes the sum, both states give 10, so set g₁(5)=10. If q₂ takes the maximum, the states require 10 and 5 respectively, so the same representation cannot answer exactly. The first success and second failure can both be retained without calling all compression useless.

BoundaryThe proof concerns only these two queries and cannot be extrapolated to unknown state domains, dynamics, or action.

Mathematical construction: a worst-case-error lower bound and an integer-output counterexampleTeaching scenario

AssumptionsA finite complete domain; the first part allows arbitrary real-valued outputs, and the second explicitly changes to integer outputs. Loss is consistently global worst-case absolute error.

Suppose f partitions four source states into two preimages whose q values are {0,4} and {6,8}. Ranges 4 and 2 give a lower bound of 2; midpoint outputs 2 and 7 give worst-case errors 2 and 1 respectively, making the global optimum 2. ε=2 is achievable; ε=1.9 is not. Separately, take a single preimage with q={0,1}: arbitrary real-valued output permits 0.5, giving optimal error 0.5; if output must be an integer, both 0 and 1 give worst-case error 1, so the half-range value is no longer achievable.

BoundaryThis is not a real measurement-error or population-risk estimate; different losses or output constraints must not be conflated.

Mathematical construction: continuation checks only reachable values, but must not lose the final answerTeaching scenario

AssumptionsOnly f(X)={u,v} is allowed as actual intermediate input; all functions are constructed, and the original final query remains q.

Let X={a,b,c}, f(a)=f(b)=u, f(c)=v, and q(a)=q(b)=0, q(c)=1. Z also contains unreachable r; set g(u)=0, g(v)=1, g(r)=99. If h(u)=A, h(v)=B, h(r)=A, the actual composition still recovers q exactly with k(A)=0 and k(B)=1; the value 99 at unreachable r causes no failure. If instead h(u)=h(v)=A, a and c merge despite having different q values, so the final task fails even though the second segment completes its local task of ‘outputting a unified label.’

BoundaryIf r becomes reachable in reality later, reassessment is required; the old-domain proof cannot simply be reused.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleEncoding unknown, unobservable, not applicable, and withheld for protection all as 0, then interpreting 0 as factual nonexistence.

What it limitsThis compresses away distinct missing-data statuses and adds an unsupported negation; both representation and conclusion require correction.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleA decoder given mean 5 secretly checks the originals and supplies maxima 10 and 5 respectively, while claiming exact recovery from the mean alone.

What it limitsThis violates the decoding-input constraint; the actual system uses a richer representation.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleThe first segment retains two positions and the second only counts them, yet the original task ‘is the first position active?’ is declared complete.

What it limitsA local task is not the final task; merging (0,1) and (1,0) leaves conflicting answers.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleContinuing to claim optimal error 0.5 for the {0,1} preimage when outputs must be integers.

What it limitsThat midpoint is not an allowed output; the actual optimal worst-case error is 1.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Use the half-range formula only for a finite nonempty domain with real-valued targets, arbitrary real-valued decoding, and global worst-case absolute error.
  • Exact recovery of q does not establish dynamic closure, feasible intervention, or satisfaction of premises by a real mapping, nor does it generate authority.
  • Preimages contain only actually reachable states; unreachable intermediate values cannot manufacture a false failure.
  • Discovering an action error does not automatically attribute it to compression loss; the rule may be wrong. If the internal representation is unknown, retain that gap.
  • Substantial task-relevant loss cannot be ‘repaired’ for the original high-impact use by switching to an easier query.

Scope and open questions

This section gives exact formal conditions and proofs, with finite constructions that can be recalculated item by item; it does not force historical events lacking complete internal-representation material into cases of a mathematical theorem.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Why does constancy within preimages suffice to define g?

  2. 2

    Why can a single preimage with q={0,4} not achieve worst-case error below 2?

  3. 3

    Does successful recovery of the total establish that the maximum can also be recovered?

  4. 4

    Why does the composition condition not constrain unreachable r?

  5. 5

    Can completing a different local task in the second segment override failure of the original final task?

  6. 6

    Can the half-range directly serve as a real-world average error rate?

Why does constancy within preimages suffice to define g?

Each nonempty preimage has a unique common target value. Defining g by that value is unambiguous and yields q when substituted for any source state.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Why can a single preimage with q={0,4} not achieve worst-case error below 2?

The sum of an output's distances to both endpoints is at least 4, so at least one distance is ≥2; midpoint 2 reaches this lower bound.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does successful recovery of the total establish that the maximum can also be recovered?

No. They are different queries; mean 5 corresponds to (0,10) and (5,5), whose maxima differ.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Why does the composition condition not constrain unreachable r?

No source state reaches r through f, so r is not an actual input in q=k∘h∘f; an expanded reachable domain requires review.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Can completing a different local task in the second segment override failure of the original final task?

No. “Task Preservation through Successive Conversions” (§4.18.4) requires preserving the same final q throughout the chain; changing the question produces only a new problem.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Can the half-range directly serve as a real-world average error rate?

No. It is worst-case absolute error in a specified finite model; average risk requires a distribution and a different loss definition.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

5.5.9Horizontal Transfer (M09) ​

In briefSuccess in a source domain gives reason to ask a better question in the target domain; it cannot answer that question on the target's behalf. Clearer mappings reveal what is comparable and what must be checked separately.

Horizontal transfer is summed up as “analogical transfer across domains.” The mappings, differences, discontinuities, prohibited mappings, the chain of responsibility at the target end, and differences in the scope of authorization must be stated. Material from the source domain only proposes candidates at the target end. Both “supported” and “null conclusion supported” must come from independent tests at the target end. If the evidence at the target end is insufficient, the status is “not yet evaluated” or “not supported or unresolved.” This insufficiency does not establish the absence of the target mechanism. An analogy creates no authorization to act in the target domain.

5.5.9Note

Understanding this section

5.5.9 Horizontal transfer (M09)

Success in a source domain gives reason to ask a better question in the target domain; it cannot answer that question on the target's behalf. Clearer mappings reveal what is comparable and what must be checked separately.

Horizontal transfer states relational mappings between source and target, not merely similar nouns. Specify source object, target object, preserved relations, key differences, possible breaks, prohibited mappings, and differences in the target's responsibility chain and in the scope of authorization. Comparability is a bounded candidate, not certification that the target claim holds.

Source-domain material can generate only target candidates. Both “supported” and “null conclusion supported” in the target require an independent test at the target end and corresponding material; “many source studies” cannot fill gaps in target object, measurement, boundaries, or comparison. Nothing carried out at the target end means “not yet evaluated”; evaluation with insufficient bridge or evidence remains “not supported or unresolved.”

Structural isomorphism need not mean a shared mechanism. Identical input-output tables can arise from different internal processes, and similar statistical ratios may have multiple causes. Transfer should propose target-domain observations or comparisons that distinguish those mechanisms, rather than seeking only support for the analogy.

Insufficient target material does not mean the target mechanism is absent. Rejection of an analogy need not overturn the original source conclusion; the mapping may break, target conditions may differ, or the task may change. Preserve each domain's known facts and conclusion boundaries, avoiding “one side fails, so delete both.”

Analogy grants no target action permission. Transferring machine-control strategies to an organization or one community's support network to another cannot copy value tradeoffs, representative standing, or intervention authority, even where descriptions resemble one another. State target responsibility chains and affected-person protections anew.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First delimit the actual scope of source-domain conclusions and the target task without enlarging source support.

  2. 2

    Construct relational mappings item by item, also listing differences, breaks, and prohibited mappings.

  3. 3

    Propose target candidates and target observations or comparisons that can distinguish alternative explanations.

  4. 4

    Obtain independent target material and determine status separately according to actual execution, the positive criterion, and the null-conclusion criteria.

  5. 5

    When an analogy fails, identify whether it limits the mapping, target claim, or source conclusion; do not impose unsupported collateral rejection.

  6. 6

    Check target responsibilities, protections, and differences in the scope of authorization; transferring knowledge cannot transfer unauthorized power.

Distinctions to keep clear

Source-domain support obtained

Material exists for the source object and conditions.

≠

Target candidate

The mapping supplies a question for testing; an independent test at the target end is still needed.

Surface or statistical similarity

Certain relations or indicators are close.

≠

Identical mechanism

Requires ruling out different processes producing similar results.

Target unknown

Not carried out or insufficiently supported.

≠

Target absent

A stronger denial that does not automatically follow from insufficient evidence.

Mathematical construction: the same static table, different intervention targetsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsTwo deterministic structural models are stipulated; target intervention replaces only the x equation, preserves c, and measurement is error-free.

The source system specifies y=x; the target system first sets hidden c to 0 or 1, then x=c and y=c. Natural observations in both systems may show only (0,0) and (1,1), but changing only x while holding c fixed in the target does not change y. Identical natural static tables do not suffice to transfer the source rule “changing x changes y” to the target.

BoundaryA formal counterexample to analogy, not a test of any actual causal system.

Teaching construction: transferring a queueing method does not transfer punitive authorityTeaching scenario

AssumptionsDomains and proposal are teaching assumptions; no claim of actual community implementation or measured effects.

A fictional laboratory predicts waiting time from task-queue length and proposes the same-named indicator for community services. Arrivals, service capacity, and waiting windows may be mapped as candidates; people's ability to exit, hidden demand, priority rules, appeals, and responsibilities differ. Even if independent target material validates prediction, this confers no permission to deny services or punish people.

BoundaryOffers no actual intervention advice; target action still requires independent value, protection, and permission conditions.

Neanderthal research explicitly warns against turning similar ratios into identical social organizationDocumented case

After comparing ratios concerning Y-chromosome and mitochondrial diversity, Skov and colleagues specifically note that similar ratios in apes and Neanderthals need not imply the same social organization: ape data have heterogeneous sources, and different processes can generate similar ratios. The paper separately uses Neanderthals' own genetic material and model comparisons to propose a female-migration explanation.

SourceSkov et al., Nature 610（2022），Genetic insights into the social organization of NeanderthalsMain: Inferring social organization, warning paragraph after the cross-species ratio comparison and adjacent model-comparison passageReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsSupports the authors' explicit limits on cross-species analogy while retaining their local explanation from target data; does not extend to all Neanderthals or political rule structures, nor retrospectively award a formal test.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleIntervening on x works in the source, and the target has identical observational correlations, so the target can do the same.

What it limitsThe same observation table can arise from a common cause; target causation needs independent material.

What does not follow

  • Independent target material concerns the target object; it is not source material relabeled and reposted.
  • Source analogies offer only bounded guidance; identical physical, social, or normative terms do not constitute cross-domain proof.
  • Preserve domain authors' actual conclusions, without retrospectively awarding eligibility for this framework's formal tests or denying their independent achievements because the framework has not certified them.

Scope and open questions

The original authors explicitly limit cross-domain similarities and separately compare target material, making this suitable for showing the distinction between candidates and target evidence.

5.6Limits of Basic Structural Concepts Across Scales ​

In briefGiving a phenomenon a concept name such as “feedback,” “memory,” or “phase” begins to clarify a question; it does not automatically establish learning, historical increment, or object conversion. Claims of different strengths need their own proportionate evidence.

The eleven basic structural concepts are definitions. They carry no empirical null models or falsification templates of their own. Four limits in particular must be held.

“Feedback and State Updating” (§3.5.7). Basic feedback requires only a return channel and a subsequent state update. It does not require a historical-increment test. A claim that feedback has mediated learning must also have corresponding evidence of an update carrier, retention across rounds, actual use, and task outcomes. A historical-increment test is added only when the claim is a historical conditional increment beyond the stated current state (see §4.5 and §6.3).

“Load, Capacity, and Recovery Margin” (§3.5.9). An instantaneous demand–capacity gap does not require a historical-increment test. Cumulative damage or delayed recovery must be checked separately against the current carrier of damage or capacity, how that carrier formed, and subsequent recovery. A historical-increment test applies only when a further claim is made about a historical increment beyond the current representation.

“Trace, Memory, and Paths” (§3.5.10). This concept only records candidate traces, their carriers, and their retention windows. It does not establish path dependence in advance. That history still provides a conditional increment after controlling for the current state must still be shown by a historical-increment test.

“Phase, Transition, and Dissolution” (§3.5.11). The basic phase pattern requires neither a historical-increment test nor a scale-closure test. Causal triggering takes a separate channel-effect test. Continuation or delayed recovery sustained by the current carrier takes evidence under §4.5. Historical-increment hysteresis beyond the current representation takes a separate historical-increment test. Object conversion takes a separate scale-closure test.

Likewise, the concept “Candidate Object” (§3.5.1) only records candidate objects and does not guarantee grouping gain in advance. The definition of “Relations and Constraints” (§3.5.5) does not establish causation. The descriptions of channels within “Flow, Channels, and Transmission” (§3.5.6) do not establish a channel effect.

5.6Note

Understanding this section

5.6 Limits of basic structural concepts across scales

Giving a phenomenon a concept name such as “feedback,” “memory,” or “phase” begins to clarify a question; it does not automatically establish learning, historical increment, or object conversion. Claims of different strengths need their own proportionate evidence.

The eleven basic structural concepts are definitions, carrying no empirical null models or falsification templates of their own. They help state objects, channels, states, and windows; complete items alone cannot obtain empirical support for the four empirical questions. Discussing an actual mechanism requires a specific question and corresponding evidence; minimum definitional conditions must not be mistaken for complete mechanism identification.

The basic feedback of “Feedback and State Updating” (§3.5.7) requires only a return channel and subsequent state update. An output observed without returning, or a return that does not change subsequent state, cannot establish effective feedback on that basis. Conversely, a transient update can constitute basic feedback without a mandatory cross-round memory or historical-increment test.

Feedback-mediated learning adds a chain beyond basic feedback: updating a locatable carrier, retaining or continually updating it across rounds, actually using it later, and corresponding evidence for predefined task outcomes. One parameter change, one success, or one archived item does not complete the chain. Carried learning does not first require additional historical increment; a historical-increment test is added only for a claim of historical conditional increment beyond the stated current state.

“Load, Capacity, and Recovery Margin” (§3.5.9) first separates instantaneous demand-capacity shortfall, accumulated damage, and delayed recovery. Demand 8 and capacity 5 now define a current shortfall of 3, not prior proof of a historical increment or long-term damage. Claiming overload causes damage and delays recovery requires tracing the current damage or capacity carrier, its formation, and subsequent recovery. Only a further need for history beyond the stated current state enters a historical-increment test.

“Trace, Memory, and Paths” (§3.5.10) states candidate traces, carriers, and retention windows without guaranteeing use of the trace or pre-establishing path dependence. Archive existence, retrieval availability, actual reading, entry into decisions, and task differences are separate links. A historical-increment test further tests historical conditional increment after controlling for the stated current state; “an old file exists” is not increment evidence.

The basic phase pattern of “Phase, Transition, and Dissolution” (§3.5.11) describes differences in operating modes without requiring a historical-increment test or a scale-closure test. Explaining what triggers a mode change requires a separate channel-effect test. Persistence or delayed recovery maintained by a current carrier follows the carrier route of 4.5; a claim of historical-increment hysteresis beyond the current representation requires a separate historical-increment test; an object-identity conversion claim requires a separate scale-closure test. A switch moving from on to off does not necessarily become another object simply because its state differs.

Three other reminders matter equally: “Candidate Object” (§3.5.1) lists a candidate object without guaranteeing support for grouping gain in advance; “Relations and Constraints” (§3.5.5) defines relations without proving causation; “Flow, Channels, and Transmission” (§3.5.6) states the descriptive items of a channel without proving its corresponding effects. Candidates are valuable, but candidate status cannot be switched into a successful conclusion.

Keep three questions separate in research across time: how the past formed a current carrier, how that carrier continues to affect the future, and whether history adds usefulness given the current representation. Independent process and comparison material may establish the first two while the third fails; failure of the third's positive gate cannot establish the first two in reverse. Formal carrier-mechanism support also requires the proportionate channel-effect test or specific test of a human empirical hypothesis that §4.5 requires, while existing domain evidence retains its own conclusions and limitations without retrospective framework eligibility.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First identify which basic structural concept is used, disclosing object, variables, channels, carriers, and window, and stating that definitions provide no empirical certification.

  2. 2

    Separate proposed conclusions into specific questions about basic feedback, learning, instantaneous shortfall, damage recovery, traces, phases, and so on.

  3. 3

    For the carrier route, trace input formation, current retention, actual use, and the future task; causal claims additionally require proportionate comparisons such as interruption/replacement.

  4. 4

    Enter a historical-increment test only for an additional historical conditional increment beyond the stated current representation; deliberate omission of known current carriers is prohibited.

  5. 5

    Enter the corresponding scale-closure test separately only for an object-conversion claim; switching modes does not itself generate identity conversion.

  6. 6

    Retain supported facts, domain conclusions, mechanism candidates, and unresolved points item by item; failure of one route neither rescues nor erases another.

  7. 7

    Action and net benefits still require separate checks; learning, feedback, and phase change do not automatically establish improvement or permission.

Distinctions to keep clear

Basic feedback

A return affecting subsequent state suffices; no persistent carrier across rounds is required.

≠

Feedback-mediated learning

Also requires evidence for retention/updating, actual use, task outcomes, and related conditions.

Current-carrier transmission

The relevant past has been written into the present state and continues to act.

≠

Historical conditional increment

Only history's additional usefulness given an explicit current state is the narrow question of the historical-increment test.

Instantaneous shortfall

The difference between current demand and capacity.

≠

Accumulated damage or delayed recovery

Involves carrier formation and recovery processes; a momentary shortfall alone cannot establish it.

Phase change

The operating mode changes within the same object.

≠

Object conversion

The corresponding definition of identity no longer holds, with material required for a formal conversion claim.

Trace preservation

A record exists in a carrier.

≠

A trace has subsequent effects

Requires evidence of use and its task relationship; archiving alone is insufficient.

Mathematical construction: transient feedback holds without established persistent learningTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAn exact state machine with fixed rules; the comparator computes and returns error from actual output. The end-of-round reset is complete, with no hidden storage; there is no actual equipment experiment.

Within one round, a fictional controller first outputs a=0 against target r=1. A comparator reads this actual output, computes e=r−a=1, returns the error signal through a channel, and updates a←a+e to 1 for the next output. At the end of every round, a is forcibly reset to 0, retaining neither parameters nor other traces. There is return and state update within a round; these rules alone cannot establish learning retained and used across rounds.

BoundaryShows feedback and learning are nonequivalent; does not claim all real controllers work this way or evaluate performance improvement.

Mathematical construction: current damage suffices to explain delayed recoveryTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe damage variable, recovery amount 1, and rule are artificial stipulations, not medical/equipment parameters; the same rule uses only current d and current u.

Let d₀=0, demand uₜ, and fixed rated capacity 5. Define fictional damage update dₜ₊₁=max(0,dₜ+max(0,uₜ−5)−1) and available capacity cₜ=max(0,5−dₜ). With input u=(8,5,5,5), d follows 0→2→1→0→0 and c follows 5→3→4→5→5. Capacity does not immediately recover when demand returns to 5, which current d and its update explain; given d and future inputs, the complete model needs no additional history.

BoundaryDelayed recovery exists in this model but does not automatically establish a historical increment; actual damage formation, measurement, and recovery still require independent evidence.

Teaching construction: a mode switch need not change the objectTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe identity criterion and the apparatus are teaching stipulations, not an actual product identification; no pass of a scale-closure test is declared.

In the definition of a fictional lamp as an object, the identity criterion specifies that the housing, wiring, and switchable apparatus continue to exist; ‘on/off’ is only an operating state. A switch input turns it from on to off, fitting a phase description without making the identity criterion fail. If a separate disassembly causes the original identity criterion no longer to hold, that is a new identity question; the earlier on/off switch cannot establish object conversion in its place.

BoundaryCheck state change, causal triggering, and object identity separately.

CAIB on the database: distinguish storage from useDocumented case

CAIB Volume I, Chapter 7, p.189 discusses NASA's Lessons Learned Information System, stating that it could have assisted risk assessment but that use by design and mission-assurance personnel was sporadic, limiting its usefulness. The new focus here is the nonequivalence of “experience records exist” and “they actually enter subsequent work,” rather than another discussion of information pathways.

SourceCAIB Volume I, Chapter 7（2003）Printed p.189, Dysfunctional Databases passage, text concerning the Lessons Learned Information SystemReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsSupports the report's bounded evaluation of usage at that time; does not say nobody ever used it, deny all organizational learning, or establish a historical increment or a formal learning mechanism on this basis alone.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleA database contains ten years of records, so the organization is declared to have learned and to exhibit historical-increment path dependence.

What it limitsPreservation does not guarantee use, task change, or an increment beyond the current representation; each requires additional evidence.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleRecovery is slow after capacity declines, so a separate historical term must be needed; in fact, current damage d fully determines recovery.

What it limitsA current carrier may explain it; delayed recovery alone is not evidence of a historical increment.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleRecording “object converted” merely because a lamp changes from on to off.

What it limitsA change of operating mode need not violate the object's definition of identity and is still less equivalent to a supported formal conversion in a scale-closure test.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleThere is no positive result from a historical-increment test, so feedback is declared never to have existed.

What it limitsThis wrongly projects failure of a narrow historical increment backward into denial of basic feedback.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Do not require a historical-increment test for all feedback or all persistent learning; only the additional-historical-increment route needs it.
  • Failure of the positive criterion of the historical-increment test establishes neither absence of historical formation nor carrier sufficiency, and does not automatically support a bounded zero conclusion.
  • In-principle expansion of current state does not mean a sufficient state has been measured in this case; actual gaps must remain visible.
  • Stipulating a complete state in a model can supply an exact counterexample, not deny omitted variables or path dependence in reality.
  • Preserve established general learning or behavioral change in domain research; do not cancel it because formal-mechanism status under this framework was not sought.

Scope and open questions

The investigation report directly distinguishes availability of experience records from actual use, making it suitable for explaining the boundary between the traces of “Trace, Memory, and Paths” and the learning chain of “Feedback and State Updating”.

In the damage example, why does capacity stay at 3 and then rise to 4 after demand returns to 5?

d previously accumulated to 2, and current d recovers by 1 each step; delayed recovery is explained by the stated carrier and requires no additional historical variable.

May support from a historical-increment test be claimed by deleting current damage d from the record and then finding that history predicts capacity?

When does “Phase, Transition, and Dissolution” separately add a channel-effect test, a historical-increment test, and a scale-closure test?

Causal triggering takes a separate channel-effect test, historical-increment hysteresis beyond the current representation a separate historical-increment test, and object conversion a separate scale-closure test; a basic pattern description does not automatically require the latter two.

Does an archive system's existence establish that its contents entered later decisions?

No. Actual availability, reading, use, and connection to the task are required; archiving supports only part of the trace/carrier claim.

Does an unevaluated formal framework mechanism cancel domain research conclusions about general learning?

No; retain the study's original object, methods, conclusions, and limitations without retrospectively granting it the status of a formal test.
