5.10Cross-Circle Relation Transformation ​

In briefTwo groups beginning to interact need not mean “scale elevation”; a person joining two circles does not mean they can represent both. First map membership and interface relations accurately, then ask what transmission, loss, and permission changes occurred.

Scale transformation and cross-circle relation transformation must be kept separate. Scale transformation asks which variables are preserved, changed, or lost for the same question between the source scale and the target scale. Cross-circle relation transformation asks how two or more candidate circles[1] stand in parallel, contain one another, overlap, bridge, compete, or form temporarily at the same or different scales. A change in relations may accompany a change in scale. Neither term can stand in for the account of the other.

An account of a cross-circle relation needs to set out, at minimum, the source of the relation, its target, the type of static relation, whether membership or interfaces serve as the basis, direction, channel, delay, threshold, time window, evidence, and counterexamples. It also sets out before-and-after snapshots. “Transformed” is used only for the outcome of a relation update. A formerly parallel relation may become bridged when a bridging party appears. An overlapping relation may become nested through institutional integration, and a temporary circle may become institutionalized or undergo dissolution. Each such transformation needs a check of whether the identity criterion is preserved. If the identity criterion no longer holds, record an object conversion. A new name must not be used to carry the old object forward.

Question to AnswerWhat to UseDistinctions to Preserve
Can an individual’s state represent a team?Aggregation (§5.5.1), the account of the scale transformation, and distributional lossTeam membership alone does not make a member’s state representative of the team
Is a team contained within an organization?Nesting (§5.5.2) and a specific basis for containmentHaving a superior in common does not imply membership containment
Are two circles associated because they share members?The overlap relation, membership mappings, and the common environmentOverlap does not by itself produce effective feedback
Does a bridging party change another circle?Network propagation (§5.5.3), a channel, and a counterfactualContact does not amount to transmission. Transmission does not amount to representation
Does a temporary group form a durable object?The identity criterion, longitudinal material about the object, and institutionalization (§5.5.5). A claim of grouping gain takes a separate grouping-gain test, and a claim of a historical conditional residual takes a separate historical-increment testTraces do not amount to institutionalization. The fact of durability need not depend on an additional historical residual

When the same actor belongs to several circles, the actor’s distinct roles, visible information, responsibilities, risks, and ability to exit in each circle need to be retained. An actor must not first be merged into a single state that is then copied to every circle. Cross-circle projection should start from local states, propagate through stated membership or interface channels, and record the loss caused by aggregation at each step.

Translation involves both tasks and permissions. Accurately relaying what someone said, helping both sides understand each other, having permission to publish that person’s exact words, and signing an agreement on their behalf are four distinct capabilities or qualifications. The same translation can suffice to book an appointment and may still be insufficient to preserve poetic rhythm or distinctions in legal status. Insufficiency for the latter task does not justify saying retroactively that the former was never completed. The limited translation that succeeds should be retained, and the meanings and rights that did not transfer with it should be stated. 〔Studies 12.10, 26.08–26.09〕

5.10Note

Understanding this section

5.10 Cross-Circle Relational Transformation

Two groups beginning to interact need not mean “scale elevation”; a person joining two circles does not mean they can represent both. First map membership and interface relations accurately, then ask what transmission, loss, and permission changes occurred.

Scale transformation asks which variables in the same task are preserved, changed, or lost from source scale SP0 to target scale SP1. Circle-relation transformation asks how candidate circles are juxtaposed, contained, overlapping, bridged, competing, or temporarily formed. Circle relations may change at the same scale or alongside scale change, but one label cannot replace the account of the other.

A cross-circle record includes at least the relation's source and target, static relation type, membership or interface baseline, direction, channel, delay, threshold, time window, evidence, counterexamples, and before/after snapshots. A result diagram alone is insufficient if the prior state is unknown, and unobserved edges cannot be drawn as nonexistent.

“Transformed” is the result of a relational update, not a static relation type alongside “juxtaposed,” “nested,” or “bridged.” Previously parallel circles may connect through a new bridge person; overlapping circles may become nested through institutional integration; temporary groups may institutionalize or dissolve. Specify the actual old and new types and evidence of change, rather than merely entering “transformed.”

Check the identity criterion during relational updates. If the original identity criterion fails, renaming cannot continue to masquerade as the same object. This section's object-conversion guidance must be read with 5.7's formal classification conditions: determining “object converted” also requires a corresponding separate test of the object-conversion step and a supported scale-closure test of the subtype for object or intervention conversion. Where material is still missing, retain an identity gap/“undetermined”; one failed check against the identity criterion must not retroactively confer conversion success.

The original table's first question asks whether an individual state can represent a team, requiring aggregation (§5.5.1), an account of the scale transformation, and distributional losses. Membership in a team establishes only membership; individual average performance or opinions cannot unconditionally substitute for the whole team. The second question asks whether a team is contained in an organization, requiring nesting (§5.5.2) and a specific containment criterion; sharing a superior does not mean one team's members are contained in another.

The third question asks why shared members matter, requiring checks of overlap, member mappings, and shared environment. Overlap itself does not establish effective feedback involving updates after information returns. The fourth asks whether a bridge person changes another circle, requiring network propagation (§5.5.3), channels, and counterfactuals. Contact is not actual transmission, and transmission is not effective representation.

The fifth question asks whether a temporary group becomes a persistent object, requiring the identity criterion, longitudinal object material, and institutionalization (§5.5.5). Further claims that grouping adds gain require a separate grouping-gain test; claims of historical residuals given the current representation require a separate historical-increment test. Keeping chat records is only a trace, not a substitute for institutionalization; persistent operation also does not necessarily require an additional historical residual.

The same actor may have different roles, visible information, responsibilities, risks, and exit capabilities in multiple circles. Propagate from local states through declared membership or interface channels, recording aggregation losses step by step. Do not first compress a person into one global score and copy it to every circle. Freedom to leave an activity within a family does not imply equivalent exit conditions in employment. This is a teaching reminder about relational distinctions, not a factual finding about any individual.

Translation also has tasks and permissions: accurate rendering, helping understanding, permission to publish original words, and representing someone in signing a contract are four different things. A translation that completes an appointment may not preserve poetic rhythm or legal identity; failures in the latter two cannot rewrite the appointment as never completed. Preserve bounded translation success, meanings not transferred, and rights not granted.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Separately define candidate circles and their identity criteria, membership/interfaces, and local roles, without presuming one overall hierarchy.

  2. 2

    Record the old static relation, direction, channel, threshold, and time window, preserving a before snapshot.

  3. 3

    Obtain an after snapshot and material on change, specifying the old and new relation types.

  4. 4

    Invoke aggregation, nesting, network propagation, institutionalization, and other transformations as the question requires; additional grouping, historical, or conversion claims carry the responsibilities of their corresponding empirical tests.

  5. 5

    For each actor, preserve differences in multi-circle roles, information, risks, responsibilities, and exit, propagating through actual channels.

  6. 6

    Check whether identity is preserved. When the identity criterion fails, do not continue by renaming; assess formal conversion independently under 5.7.

  7. 7

    For translation, evaluate task completion separately from publication/representation permissions, preserving bounded successes and losses.

Distinctions to keep clear

Circle-relation update

Changes in relations such as juxtaposition, containment, overlap, or bridging.

≠

Scale-profile change

Axis-by-axis comparison of the nine axes and what is preserved/changed/lost.

Shared member

The same person belongs to multiple sets.

≠

Effective feedback

Also requires a return channel and subsequent state updating.

Transmit content

Information actually arrives through a channel.

≠

Eligibility to represent or publish

A separate question of authorization and use.

Transformed

A result marker for a before/after relational update.

≠

Static relation type

Whether the relation at that time is juxtaposition, bridging, nesting, or another type.

Identity criterion fails

Identity and what cannot be carried forward require reassessment.

≠

Formal conversion supported

Also requires satisfying 5.7 and the responsibilities of the corresponding scale-closure test of the subtype for object or intervention conversion; names alone cannot establish it.

Mathematical construction: overlapping without nesting, and without automatic feedbackTeaching scenario

AssumptionsComplete finite membership sets, with entirely fictional people; information transmission occurs only under the separately stated condition.

Let A={A-person,B-person} and B={B-person,C-person}, with intersection {B-person}. Since A-person∉B and C-person∉A, neither contains the other. If the assumptions provide no evidence that B-person relays messages or updates after return, only membership overlap can be recorded; an effective A→B→A feedback loop cannot be added. If B-person is later observed passing A's notice to B, this adds only one transmission fact and still establishes neither return nor representative authority.

BoundaryAn intersection cannot establish that an actual person relayed information or was entrusted to act.

Teaching construction: local roles are not copiedTeaching scenario

AssumptionsRoles and material are assumed; no actual personal privacy or delegation is involved.

Fictional B-person organizes materials in a reading group and serves as a reviewer in a work group. Private notes visible in the reading group do not automatically become material publishable by the work group; review duties also do not automatically extend to other reading-group members. State visible information, duties, risks, and exit conditions separately in both settings, then check the specific interface permitted to cross the boundary.

BoundaryThe example decides no disclosure or authorization itself; it only shows that local role arrangements cannot be merged.

Teaching construction: appointment translation completed, publication and contracting still unsupportedTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe linguistic content, people, and appointment are constructed; no actual translation experiment is claimed.

Suppose a translator accurately conveys the time in “meet at three on Tuesday afternoon” to the other party, and both complete an appointment arrangement on that basis. This supports only the bounded task; it does not authorize publication of the entire original statement or signing a contract for the speaker. If the original is also a rhythmic poem, failure of the appointment translation to preserve meter does not cancel successful transmission of the time.

BoundaryThe four capabilities or statuses require separate checking; task success does not become permission.

A distant case and a water-delivery channel: a concrete bridge beyond the geographic circleDocumented case

Snow records that a woman in Hampstead had not visited Broad Street for months, yet customarily had water from that pump delivered daily by cart. The additional observation here is that a concrete material interface may exist beyond the boundary of a residential location; contact cannot be assessed solely by neighborhood boundaries.

SourceJohn Snow（1855）Printed p. 44, passage about the Hampstead woman and daily water delivery by cartReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThese are clues concerning water delivery and contact recorded by Snow from family accounts. They do not establish every transmission mechanism, identify the deliverer as residents' representative, or confer arbitrary authority to act.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleA bridge person knows both groups and is therefore designated their official representative.

What it limitsContact, transmission, and valid delegation are three distinct responsibilities.

What does not follow

  • Membership, aggregate representation, transmission effects, and authorization cannot replace one another.
  • Traces of a temporary group differ from persistent institutional facts, and the latter are not automatically justified.
  • Multiple memberships cannot be covered by one global state; local risks and exit conditions especially must be preserved.
  • Insufficiency of translation for one task cannot cancel a result actually achieved in another independent task.
  • The relational edges in this section's constructions are not actual organizational charts and provide no real authorization to act as a representative.

Scope and open questions

The actual account provides a specific interface across geographic boundaries. This passage discusses only bridges and boundaries, without recalculating effects or claiming authorization.

What is the relation between A={A-person,B-person} and B={B-person,C-person}?

Membership overlaps without mutual containment; this alone supplies no evidence of transmission, feedback, or representative authority.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Can the original object identity be retained after bridging?

Check whether the identity criterion holds. If it fails, retain the identity question; formal conversion is assessed separately under 5.7 and the corresponding scale-closure test and cannot automatically be recorded as successful.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

How should an accurate appointment translation that fails to preserve poetic meter be reported?

Preserve bounded success on the appointment task and separately report loss on the poetic-meter task; neither task can erase the other.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Do persistent institutional facts necessarily require an additional historical residual first?

No. Persistent carrier/institutional facts may have independent grounds; only an extra historical increment beyond the current representation requires a separate historical-increment test.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does accurate rendering prove permission to publish the original words?

No. Content competence and publication permission are separate.

5.10.1Three Kinds of Transformation Must Be Kept Separate ​

In briefA passage that is aggregated, translated, and sent into another circle may change scale, relations, and expression simultaneously. Separating them reveals what each step preserved and where a problem occurred.

Scale transformation asks which variables are preserved, changed, or lost for the same question between one scale profile and another. Cross-circle relation transformation asks how parallelism, containment, overlap, bridging, competition, or temporary relations among candidate circles are updated. Representational or discursive recasting (§3.4.1) asks how content with an identified source enters the vocabulary, variables, or expressions of the target task. All three can occur together, but they must be split apart and accounted for separately, in order.

Recasting needs its own account of what it preserves, changes, and loses. It can use the scale transformations “Network Propagation,” “Compression or Abstraction,” and “Horizontal Transfer,” or others (§5.5). Each of these operations has its own account, and they are linked according to their respective inputs, outputs, criteria, and failure conditions. A further transformation must not be counted merely because a name differs, and failures of different operations must not be merged into a single overall status.

5.10.1Note

Understanding this section

5.10.1 Three Types of Transformation Must Be Separated

A passage that is aggregated, translated, and sent into another circle may change scale, relations, and expression simultaneously. Separating them reveals what each step preserved and where a problem occurred.

Scale transformation compares source scale SP0 and target scale SP1 and tracks preservation, change, and loss of variables for the same question. Circle-relation transformation compares updates in juxtaposition, containment, overlap, bridging, competition, or temporary relations. Representational/discursive recasting asks how sourced content enters the vocabulary, variables, or expression of a target task. Their inputs and outputs may be connected, but they are not identical.

All three may occur simultaneously, but must be separated into ordered records. Aggregating personal records into a team mean, writing the mean as a plain-language summary, and then sending it to another department through a new channel may respectively involve scale, recasting, and a circle interface. Preserve correspondence between adjacent objects, content, and uses; “overall communication succeeded” must not conceal loss at an individual step.

Recasting needs its own account, but it is not a tenth transformation created by a new name. It can use “Network Propagation,” “Compression or Abstraction,” “Horizontal Transfer,” or other scale transformations; each transformation used is still accounted for by its own inputs, outputs, criteria, and failure conditions. A different question to account for does not automatically increase the amount of evidence.

Separation also helps preserve local results. A summary may be faithful but not yet received by the target circle; information may arrive while the summary has lost a crucial modality; membership relations may be updated while the scale comparison for the same task remains unknown. Different failures cannot be merged into a vague overall status, nor may success in one rescue the others.

Order also affects conclusions. Preserving whether any individual falls below a threshold before aggregation differs from first taking the mean and then asking whether that mean falls below the threshold. Calling both “summarizing” cannot erase noncommutativity. After order changes, recheck tasks and losses along the new record chain.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Write one explicit question each for scale, circle relations, and the recasting of content.

  2. 2

    Specify each record's source/target, input/output, use, preserved items, and failure conditions.

  3. 3

    If they occur together, connect them in actual order and check consistency between adjacent objects and content.

  4. 4

    Account for the transformations used separately; a new name does not add a transformation.

  5. 5

    Report actual statuses and losses individually, retaining local successes and unresolved questions.

  6. 6

    When order or the target task changes, check the new chain separately rather than carrying over the original success label.

Distinctions to keep clear

Scale transformation

Preservation/change of the nine axes and variables for the same task.

≠

Circle-relation transformation

An update in the relation type between candidate circles.

Representational recasting

Content enters the target expression/task with an account of semantic preservation.

≠

New transformation

Having a separate name cannot create a new transformation from nothing.

Ordered chain

Each step's own status and correspondence with adjacent steps.

≠

Overall success label

May conceal independent failures at different steps.

Mathematical construction: two orders under the same label “summarizing”Teaching scenario

AssumptionsA specific counterexample in a complete two-unit domain, with exact values and a final task fixed beforehand; logical OR and averaging are different operations.

Two fictional units have values (0,10), and the final question is ‘is any unit below 2?’ Route one checks the threshold separately, obtaining (true,false), then takes the logical OR, yielding true. Route two first takes the mean 5 and then tests 5<2, yielding false; it actually answers ‘is the mean below 2?’ and has changed the question. The two routes cannot share task success merely because both are called summaries.

BoundaryThis only shows that operations/tasks must not be conflated; it does not claim that a real organization processed them this way.

Teaching construction: separate successful expression from unresolved deliveryTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe records, teams, and acknowledgment situation are constructed; no real maintenance or sending operation occurred.

The fictional source content consists of three maintenance records. Review confirms that the summary faithfully retains specified fault types and uncertainties, but the channel sending it to another team has no acknowledgment or other evidence of arrival. Support for the recasting task may be retained while delivery remains unresolved. Missing delivery evidence does not retrospectively make the summary unfaithful, nor does a correct summary establish that the recipient received it.

BoundaryActual understanding and subsequent action require separate checks; a sending record itself need not establish understanding.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleThe summary is correct, so the receiving circle's relation updating and understanding are complete.

What it limitsRecasting, transmission, and relation updating each require corresponding evidence; status does not transfer automatically.

Teaching counterexampleGiving recasting a new name adds an all-purpose transformation beyond the nine scale transformations.

What it limitsA separate account does not automatically expand the list of transformations; specify the transformations actually used and their composition.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleBoth orders are called summarization, so opposite results need no explanation.

What it limitsThe original final task and operation orders differ; precisely locate the changed question or collapsed information.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Reusing the same material in three kinds of transformation does not increase the count of independent observations.
  • Recasting guarantees neither distortion nor losslessness; check it against the task.
  • Completed transmission does not mean target understanding, nor does understanding mean permission to publish or sign a contract.
  • Different names alone do not establish three actual operations; specific inputs, outputs, and changes must be identifiable.

Scope and open questions

This unit distinguishes three types of transformation using constructions about operation order and content handoff, without adding unwarranted claims of complete execution in historical events.

  3. 3

  4. 4

If a team mean is summarized and sent to a new department, which questions must at least be asked?

Evaluate separately, in ordered records, whether the mean's scale/aggregation preserves the task, whether summary recasting preserves semantics, and whether the cross-department interface actually transmits.

5.10.2Reviewing Recasting Loss ​

In briefChecking recasting cannot ask only ‘can it be translated back?’ Ask whether the distinctions needed by the target task remain, whether rules were used correctly, and where review can return when anomalies appear.

If two source states that can be distinguished in the source task cannot be distinguished in the target representation, record a task-relevant loss for that distinction. An identity mapping, reversible encoding, or mapping sufficient for the target task may yield no detected relevant loss. The rule is therefore “do not assume losslessness in advance.” It does not say that a mapping is “necessarily lossy.”

Review ItemMinimum QuestionDistinctions to Preserve
PreservationWhich facts, relations, modalities, rights, or uncertainties must stay the same?Preserving a title does not amount to preserving its semantics
ChangeWhich formats, units, levels of granularity, or expressions may change?Permitting change does not permit arbitrary changes in meaning
CollapseWhich differences at the source end are merged at the target end?Collapsing a difference does not imply that it is absent at the source end
OmissionWhat was left out of the target representation, and why?Withholding for protection does not amount to absence
AdditionWhich explanations, inferences, or target variables does the conversion produce?Adding a variable does not amount to discovering a real-world entity
ReturnWhen an anomaly occurs, which parent record (the record one level up from which it directly comes) or which arrangement is revisited?Returning only reopens review. It does not patch what has already been done

Round-trip reconstruction, from the target representation back to the source representation, can serve as a test but is insufficient by itself. A conversion may appear to round-trip by using hidden source records while failing to preserve the semantics of the target task. A one-way summary, by contrast, may be sufficient for the specified task. Review must return to the items to preserve that were stated in advance, the tolerances for loss, and the results at the target end.

Whether the target representation retains a needed distinction and whether the actual rule uses it correctly are two separate judgments. An error in acting on the representation does not by itself establish a recasting loss. If the distinction is still discernible but used incorrectly, record the gap in the rule or its execution. Representational loss and execution errors can also coexist. Their grounds should then be stated separately, and other local results that have already been established should be retained.

When both kinds of failure occur, the same unavoidable error should not be counted again as an additional failure of the rule. If the target answer is nonunique within a preimage (the source states mapped to the same target representation), no deterministic rule using only the current representation can answer correctly for all of its source states. This by itself establishes that the representation is insufficient. If the target answer is unique in another nonempty preimage but the actual rule gives the wrong answer, that case alone suffices to show, independently, that the rule is in error. When it is unclear what representation is actually used internally, the original material’s continued public availability does not establish that those implementing the rule had grasped the distinction at the time. The existence of material, timely access to it, and actual use must be checked separately.

5.10.2Note

Understanding this section

5.10.2 Reviewing recasting loss

Checking recasting cannot ask only ‘can it be translated back?’ Ask whether the distinctions needed by the target task remain, whether rules were used correctly, and where review can return when anomalies appear.

If two source states that must be distinguished for the declared source/target task are merged into the same target-representation value, record that task-relevant loss. Loss is relative to the task and preservation requirements; shorter sentences are not necessarily distortions. Identity mappings, reversible encodings, or one-way summaries sufficient for the current query may have no relevant loss. The principle is to presume neither losslessness nor inevitable loss.

The first of the six review items, ‘preservation,’ asks which facts, relations, modalities, rights, and uncertainties must remain unchanged. Identical titles do not imply identical semantics. Changing ‘may fail’ to ‘has failed’ changes modality even when all keywords remain. The second, ‘change,’ asks which formats, units, granularities, and expressions may change; permission to change units does not permit changing numerical meaning or scope of application.

The third, ‘collapse,’ asks which source differences are merged; this cannot establish that those differences do not exist. The fourth, ‘omission,’ asks what did not enter the target and why; information withheld for protection retains that status and cannot become ‘there is no such content.’ The fifth, ‘addition,’ asks which explanations, inferences, or target variables the transformation introduces; creating a variable name does not discover a real entity.

The sixth, ‘return,’ must specify which parent record, original, or arrangement to revisit when an anomaly appears, and which premise to check. Returning only reopens review. Finding the correct version, issuing an explanation, or deciding to improve later cannot make errors caused by what has already been done disappear. Repair, restoration, and their verification are explicit subsequent actions.

Round-trip reconstruction can be a test, but is neither sufficient nor necessary. If a reconstructor secretly consults a hidden original, even word-perfect recovery does not establish that the target representation alone retains task semantics. Conversely, a sum summary that cannot reconstruct the complete source state may still answer the total exactly. Return to predefined preservation requirements, loss tolerances, and target-side results.

Whether a representation retains distinctions and whether actual rules use them correctly are separate judgments. If the target record explicitly distinguishes 0 from 1 but the executor treats both as 0, that is a rule or execution problem. A wrong final action does not alone establish lossy representational compression. Both failure types can coexist and each needs its own proof.

When both coexist, the same unavoidable error must not also be counted as an additional rule fault. If target answers are nonunique within a preimage, any deterministic rule reading only the current representation cannot be correct for all states; this already establishes representational insufficiency. If another nonempty preimage has a unique target answer but the actual rule still outputs the wrong answer, that is enough on its own to prove the rule wrong. This does not require every real failure to fit a unique classification of this kind.

The actual executor's internal representation at the time may be unknown. Availability of the original today does not establish timely access then, much less actual comprehension or use. Material existence, timely access, and actual use must be checked separately. Retain these gaps to avoid retrospectively attributing every error either to compression or to individual execution.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Predefine the task, distinctions to preserve, and loss tolerance; do not switch to an easier task after seeing results.

  2. 2

    List preservation, change, collapse, omission, addition, and return in order, with reasons and sources for each.

  3. 3

    Check whether identical target representations correspond to different task answers; if they conflict, identify the affected task and scope.

  4. 4

    Limit decoding inputs during reconstruction tests, excluding hidden originals or identity labels; do not require recovery of every irrelevant detail.

  5. 5

    Separately check how actual rules use retained distinctions, proving execution errors independently.

  6. 6

    When both failure types coexist, distinguish unavoidable loss from additional errors without counting the same loss twice.

  7. 7

    Retain gaps when internal representation or timely access is unknown. After returning, create new repair/review records without altering the results of what has already been done.

Distinctions to keep clear

Task-relevant loss

Distinctions needed by the target are merged or omitted by the representation.

≠

Any compression

May preserve the current task without relevant loss.

Reconstruction genuinely from the representation alone

The decoder uses only declared inputs.

≠

Backfilling with a hidden original

Does not establish that the target representation alone is sufficient.

Insufficient representation

The same preimage requires different answers.

≠

Additional rule error

Using a rule incorrectly in a preimage with a unique answer can prove on its own that the rule is wrong.

Return for review

Recheck the parent record and arrangement.

≠

Completed repair

Requires actual correction of the object or consequences and verification, not just changed wording.

Material exists now

A reviewer can inspect it now.

≠

It was available in time and used then

Requires contemporaneous access, input, and execution evidence.

Mathematical construction: a false round trip and a sufficient one-way summaryTeaching scenario

AssumptionsFinite complete domains and deterministic tasks; the first example explicitly has a hidden input, while the second asks only for the sum.

Let X={a,b}, target q(a)=0 and q(b)=1, and compression f(a)=f(b)=z. If the supposed reconstructor retrieves original x from a hidden log, it can of course output a or b, but its actual input is (z,x), not z alone, so it cannot establish f's sufficiency. In another example, X={(0,2),(1,1)}, and the summary stores only sum 2. It cannot reconstruct the original pair but answers total q=2 exactly. The examples respectively show that an apparent round trip is insufficient and a complete round trip is unnecessary.

BoundaryThis does not deny that genuinely reversible encoding preserves source information; actual budgets and semantic use still require separate checks.

Mathematical construction: two failure types coexist without double countingTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThree uniformly distributed states, binary answers, zero-one loss, and decoding that reads only f; there are no real population or reader data.

Let three states a, b, and c be equally probable solely to calculate a teaching error rate. Representation f(a)=f(b)=0 and f(c)=1, with target q=(0,1,1). The actual rule is g(0)=0 and g(1)=0, so a is correct while b and c are wrong. Preimage 0 contains answers 0 and 1; any deterministic rule must err on at least one, producing an unavoidable 1/3. Preimage 1 contains only c, whose unique answer is 1, yet outputs 0, adding an independent rule error of 1/3. Changing g(1)=1 fixes c but still cannot fix both a and b. The optimal total error rate is 1/3; the original actual rate is 2/3.

BoundaryProbabilities are assumed calculation weights, not actual risk estimates; a's local correctness is not erased by other errors.

Teaching construction: returning to a parent record does not mean an old action has been repairedTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe content, judgments, and consequences are hypothetical; no real action occurred.

A fictional summary omits ‘applies only under condition C.’ An anomaly is later found, and returning to the parent record reveals the restriction. Review of the summary and its uses can now reopen, and a target expression containing the condition can be rebuilt. Old judgments already made on the unconditional statement still require individual review; consequences, if any, require separately arranged authorized correction.

BoundaryReturn is an entry point to review, not a fact of completed restoration.

The CAIB briefing case: content location, meaning, and actual use require separate checksDocumented case

On p.191, CAIB analyzes a debris-assessment briefing: ‘conservatism’ in the title refers to the selected test model, not an assurance that damage was safe; an important warning about exceeding the test data's range appears at the bottom of the slide. This section adds the observation that the warning was not entirely absent, while information priority, wording, reception, and use could still pose problems.

Scope and limitsThis supports the report's analysis of this briefing's expression. It does not reconstruct every decision-maker's entire internal representation, treat one slide as the accident's sole cause, or attribute every information error to unavoidable compression.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

What it limitsRetaining a literal title does not preserve modal semantics; record the task-relevant change.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Do not broadly declare every recasting inevitably lossy, or guarantee preservation of all semantics/authority from a successful round trip.
  • One unavoidable error in the same mixed preimage cannot be counted twice as representational loss and an independent rule defect.
  • An added statistical variable is only a candidate explanatory or measurement tool, not automatically a root cause or entity.
  • Being able to look back today does not imply availability before the original action; if this cannot be confirmed, do not invent the executor's mental state.
  • All numerical examples are finite constructions, not measurements of real people's error rates.

Scope and open questions

The original report discusses both where information still appears and ambiguity in its wording, making it suitable for illustrating why a loss review cannot merely check keyword presence. It does not claim to know executors' complete internal states.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    If the same target value corresponds to source answers 0 and 1, can that value alone give every answer correctly?

  2. 2

    Which point in the three-state example independently establishes rule error?

  3. 3

  4. 4

  5. 5

If the same target value corresponds to source answers 0 and 1, can that value alone give every answer correctly?

No. Deterministic decoding supplies only one answer; this by itself proves the representation insufficient.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Which point in the three-state example independently establishes rule error?

Preimage 1, containing c, has unique answer 1, but the actual rule gives 0; this differs from the unavoidable conflict in preimage 0.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Why is error still nonzero after correcting g(1)=1?

Preimage 0 still merges a and b's different answers, so only one can be correct, with a minimum error of 1/3.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does inability to reconstruct the complete original necessarily mean the task cannot be completed?

Not necessarily. A summary may suffice for a specified query, such as only asking for the total of two numbers.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does finding an omitted item by returning to the parent record automatically repair what has already been done?

No. It only reopens review; old judgments and consequences require separate review, correction, and verification of completion.

5.10.3Effective Variables, Closure, and Returning in Response to Residuals ​

In briefA compressed indicator answering well today need not independently advance the state tomorrow. Effective variables must be tied to tasks and horizons; when residuals appear, first check omissions and model conditions rather than rushing to name a new entity.

An effective variable is a candidate variable proposed for a target scale or task in order to compress the state and improve an explanation, foresight[2], or comparison of options fixed in advance. Proposing an effective variable must at the same time state the object, scale, time window, and task it addresses, how it is measured, the simple baseline it is compared with, how large its error is, when it fails, and when it is retired. “Effective” does not mean that the variable is a real entity, a root cause, a universally applicable variable, or a basis for authorization.

The target representation carries no presumption of dynamic closure. For static descriptions or questions at the same scale, first check sources, conversion rules, and answers to the task, using the conditional formal propositions “Task Recovery” (§4.18.1) and “Task Preservation through Successive Conversions” (§4.18.4) when necessary. Check formal dynamical models for closure under the conditional formal proposition “Closure under Dynamics and Admissible Interventions” (§4.18.2), and obtain separate evidence for their correspondence to reality. For a descriptive mapping, the items that belong only to empirical tests do not apply and may be marked “not applicable” with reasons. A corresponding scale-closure test, with its positive criterion and null-conclusion criterion, is needed only when seeking formal empirical support under §4.6 for scale closure, object conversion, or intervention conversion. A scale change must not be fabricated to fill in every item. Failure to find a significant increment does not by itself establish closure. When an increment occurs, record the corresponding impact as a candidate for memory, noise, hysteresis, an unresolved term, or a residual. The shape alone must not be used to name a new entity.

The scale transformation record (§5.7) must state the target task under the two aspects “Identity and purpose” and “Semantics.” Under the three aspects “Transformation,” “Evidence,” and “Loss,” it must state which parent representation (the representation one level up from which the new representation directly comes) is used, which differences were collapsed, where to return when an anomaly occurs, the result of the reconstruction test, and the candidate effective variables at the target end. If the relevant information is missing, retain an explicit missingness status. A completely filled-in table must not be taken to establish that all of the source semantics have been preserved.

5.10.3Note

Understanding this section

5.10.3 Effective variables, closure, and return prompted by residuals

A compressed indicator answering well today need not independently advance the state tomorrow. Effective variables must be tied to tasks and horizons; when residuals appear, first check omissions and model conditions rather than rushing to name a new entity.

An effective variable is a candidate proposed for a target scale or task, intended to compress states or improve predefined explanation, foresight, or comparison of options. It must be tied to an object, scale, time window, task, measurement, simple baseline, errors, and failure and retirement conditions. A ‘resilience,’ ‘risk,’ or ‘coordination’ score without those ties is just a name, not a validated universal property.

Effectiveness is a bounded judgment for a specified use, not discovery of a real entity, root cause, universal variable, or basis for authorization. Even improved prediction must be distinguished from causal explanation and permission to act. When tasks or environments change, or measurements fail, review under the failure/retirement conditions rather than continuing to generalize from old performance.

For static descriptions and same-scale queries, first check sources, rules, and task answers, using the conditional formal propositions “Task Recovery” (§4.18.1) and “Task Preservation through Successive Conversions” (§4.18.4) where needed. A target representation that accurately calculates the current total need not determine the next total alone. Formal dynamic closure uses “Closure under Dynamics and Admissible Interventions” (§4.18.2): source states with the same original representation must still yield the same target representation as each other after updating under the same fixed dynamics; the representation's numerical value need not remain unchanged across the update.

If this condition holds, define the macro update by the common next-step representation within each preimage. If two source states share a current representation but have different next-step targets, a deterministic macro update cannot be correct for both. Real mappings additionally require independent evidence about objects, measurements, dynamics, and permitted actions; formal proof cannot establish that reality satisfies the premises.

For descriptive mappings, the items that belong only to empirical tests may be marked “not applicable” with reasons. Only applications under §4.6 for formal empirical support for scale closure or object/intervention conversion enter the positive criterion and the null-conclusion criterion of the corresponding scale-closure test. Do not fabricate scale changes merely to fill in these items, or force every static summary to become a transformation experiment.

Failure to find significant increment does not automatically establish closure: the comparison may lack power, precision, or necessary state information. If increment appears, first record it as a candidate involving memory, noise, hysteresis, unresolved terms, or residuals, then examine competing explanations; a long-tailed or oscillating curve cannot directly be named a new entity. A residual may simply reflect the current projection merging relevant differences; an unknown mechanism cannot be turned into a historical ontology.

The unified record must explicitly state the target task within use and semantics, and retain parent representations, merged differences, return locations, reconstruction tests, and candidate target-effective variables under conversions, evidence, and losses. Use explicit missing statuses for absent material. Complete items do not establish preservation of all source semantics, and returning does not retrospectively revise what has already been done.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Bind variable candidates to object/scale/time/task/measurement/baseline/error and failure/retirement conditions.

  2. 2

    First check whether the static task is recoverable from the representation; across segments, check preservation of the same final query.

  3. 3

    For dynamics, fix source dynamics or permitted actions and compare the updated target representations of source states sharing a representation.

  4. 4

    Separate proof of formal closure from satisfaction of premises by a real-world mapping; obtain evidence under the corresponding requirements when a formal scale-closure test is required.

  5. 5

    Even without positive increment, check the null-conclusion criteria. On finding a residual, first list candidates and competing explanations rather than directly creating entities.

  6. 6

    Return along parent representations to inspect merged differences; propose additional variables and revalidate if necessary.

  7. 7

    Reassess through the lifecycle when use or conditions change, retaining the old task's successes/failures and losses.

Distinctions to keep clear

Static task sufficiency

The current representation answers the specified q.

≠

Dynamical closure

The current representation suffices to give the next target representation under the declared dynamics.

Candidate effective variable

A compressed variable proposed as useful for the bound task.

≠

Real entity or root cause

A stronger ontological/causal claim requiring independent evidence.

Residual increment

The current model/representation leaves something unexplained.

≠

Additional historical entity

Cannot be established directly from a residual's shape or name.

The formal condition for dynamic closure holds

Provable within the given mathematical dynamics and domain.

≠

Support from a real-world scale-closure test

Requires the corresponding formal test and actual object/mapping/comparison material.

Mathematical construction: an accurate current total without next-step closureTeaching scenario

AssumptionsComplete nine-state domain, exact integer lengths, fixed work-conserving rule, no new tasks, and (r)₊=max(r,0).

Two queue lengths x=(q₁,q₂) range over {0,1,2}², with representation s=q₁+q₂. With no new arrivals each step, each nonempty queue processes exactly 1 item and an empty queue none, so F(x)=((q₁−1)₊,(q₂−1)₊). Source states (2,0) and (1,1) both have s=2, giving an entirely accurate current total; their next states are (1,0) and (0,0), with totals 1 and 0. Any deterministic macro-update reading only s=2 can supply only one value, so this representation is not closed under F.

BoundaryA purely formal counterexample, not an actual queueing experiment or a scale-closure test; it does not imply that all total representations lack closure.

Mathematical construction: adding the maximum gives bounded closureTeaching scenario

AssumptionsOnly two queues, the same fixed service quantity 1, no arrivals, and the same admissible domain as before; ordered pair (s′,m′) is explicitly distinguished from queue state (q₁,q₂).

Retain z=(s,m), where m=max(q₁,q₂), so the shorter queue has length s−m. The fixed service rule directly gives m′=(m−1)₊ and s′=(m−1)₊+(s−m−1)₊. Swapping queue positions leaves z unchanged and also yields the same next z′, allowing a macro-update to be defined by this formula. For (2,0), (s,m)=(2,2) and next representation (s′,m′)=(1,1); for queue state (1,1), (s,m)=(2,1) and next representation (s′,m′)=(0,0). The added m restores a distinction needed by these dynamics without preserving which position has the longer queue.

BoundaryPosition-dependent arrivals or a task asking which queue is too long require additional information; a closure proof grants no authority to act.

Teaching construction: treat residuals as candidates before positing entities from shapeTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe preceding examples have known rules; the real-world analogy explicitly lacks observations and claims no discovered cause.

Suppose a model predicts the next step using only total s and yields a stable residual. Returning to parent-state records to examine merged queue allocation m permits a candidate explanation of “omitted current allocation.” In the preceding complete models, adding m explains the difference without a separate “historical-inertia entity.” If real m has not been measured, only list the candidate and gather material; do not copy the model's answer into reality.

BoundaryA formal possibility cannot deny actual historical effects, nor may known m be deliberately omitted to manufacture a historical increment.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleAccurate computation of a mean or total is used to declare compressed dynamics closed.

What it limitsStatic task recovery is not dynamic closure; the same s=2 can produce different next totals.

Teaching counterexampleAfter adding m establishes closure under a fixed service rule, the same conclusion is applied to arbitrary position-dependent arrivals.

What it limitsPermitted dynamics have changed beyond the original proof's scope; recheck.

Teaching counterexampleA residual curve has a long-term shape, so it is named a universal memory entity.

What it limitsShape can only suggest candidates; examine measurement, current omissions, noise, and actual historical increment.

What does not follow

  • Formal dynamics cannot merely say “each queue processes at most 1 item” while calculating a determinate next step; this example explicitly processes exactly 1 item in each nonempty queue.
  • Closure under fixed dynamics does not guarantee closure after service rules change, new tasks arrive, or permitted interventions change.
  • Added variables may preserve only task-required distinctions, without recovering every position or source detail.
  • Absence of significant positive increment is not a closure zero conclusion; sufficiency and sensitivity still require testing.
  • Without relevant residual evidence, remain unresolved; variable names do not supply entities or permission.

Scope and open questions

This unit addresses exact formal closure, using a complete two-queue model for proof and repair; it does not declare that real systems without complete-state/dynamics material satisfy the condition for dynamic closure or are supported by a scale-closure test.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Why do two queue states with the same s=2 establish nonclosure?

  2. 2

    Why can the shorter queue be recovered after adding m?

  3. 3

    Does closure here require s to remain constant forever?

  4. 4

    Can preserving (s,m) identify which queue is longer?

  5. 5

    Is a purely descriptive record necessarily incomplete without a scale-closure test?

  6. 6

    Does finding no significant residual automatically establish closure?

Why do two queue states with the same s=2 establish nonclosure?

The same fixed F gives totals 1 and 0, making a uniquely correct next total for s=2 impossible.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Why can the shorter queue be recovered after adding m?

With total s and maximum m, the other queue length is s−m; next total and maximum are therefore calculable from (s,m).

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does closure here require s to remain constant forever?

No. Source states originally sharing a representation need only yield the same target representation after updating; the representation may change over time.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Can preserving (s,m) identify which queue is longer?

No. Swapped positions still share the representation; add the relevant distinction if the task needs position.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Is a purely descriptive record necessarily incomplete without a scale-closure test?

Not necessarily. The items that belong only to empirical tests may be inapplicable with reasons; satisfying formal and descriptive conditions supports their corresponding bounded judgments.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does finding no significant residual automatically establish closure?

No. Proportionate sufficiency/equivalence, power or sensitivity, tolerance, and the other null-conclusion criteria are still required; inadequate detection may leave the result unresolved.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

5.11Representing Parallelism and Nesting Together ​

In briefA tree showing “who is below whom” usually expresses only one relation. In reality, the same pair of objects may simultaneously exchange messages, borrow resources, and compete, with relations existing only for certain periods. These edges need separate preservation.

Real-world structures cannot be reduced to a single hierarchical tree. Local containment relations can coexist with lateral networks, membership overlap, competition for resources, and bridging through platforms. They are represented by a directed multigraph of relations. Each node keeps the definition of its own object, and each edge keeps the definition of its own relation. “Higher layer” denotes only a particular relation of containment, jurisdiction, or aggregation. It carries no implication of greater reality, correctness, or authority.

When several circles share an environment but have no direct channel, the model retains a node for the common conditions and must not invent a direct edge between the circles. When a channel is open only within the time window of an event, its edge has a start time and an end time. When different relations run in opposite directions, draw separate edges. This makes it possible to determine after an event which relation actually changed, without redrawing the whole structure as a story told after the fact.

5.11Note

Understanding this section

5.11 Simultaneous representation of parallel and nested relations

A tree showing “who is below whom” usually expresses only one relation. In reality, the same pair of objects may simultaneously exchange messages, borrow resources, and compete, with relations existing only for certain periods. These edges need separate preservation.

Local containment can coexist with lateral networks, overlapping membership, resource competition, and platform bridging. A single hierarchy tree suits a specific containment relation but may remove multiple affiliations, lateral connections, or return channels. The source does not say hierarchy trees are always useless; it says they cannot stand for all of reality's structure.

A directed multirelational graph permits multiple types of edge between the same nodes. Each node retains its own complete definition as an object, including its identity criterion, boundaries, and identity grounds. Each edge retains its own definition of the relation, including type, direction, channel, time window, and evidence. Neither what a node is nor what an edge means can be guessed from graphic position.

“Upper level” indicates only a particular containment, jurisdiction, or aggregation relation, not greater reality, correctness, or authority. A jurisdiction edge additionally needs corresponding valid permission material; placing a node at the top of a page does not generate authorization for it. Physical position, epistemic reliability, and normative eligibility cannot be inferred directly from vertical placement in a graph.

When objects share an environment without a direct channel, retain a common-condition node rather than inventing direct edges between circles. Synchronous changes in two circles may result from a common input. If existence of a direct channel is unknown, state that and the sampling boundary; “not measured” cannot become demonstrated absence of an edge.

Channels open only during an event window need start and end times. Permanent membership containment and temporary message channels may share a graph but must have different temporal attributes. Closing a communication edge after an event does not mean the two objects dissolved or all their relations changed.

Create separate edges for different relations with opposite directions. For example, A sends information to B while B sends requests to A. Though connecting the same objects, these cannot be merged into “mutual relation” at the cost of effect direction. If A also sends supplies to B, that is a third relation needing its own capacity, conditions, and evidence; the information edge cannot count for it.

Only after retaining before/after snapshots and each edge's identity can one ask which particular relation an event added, removed, or changed, and which nodes still satisfy their original identity criterion. Do not redraw the whole graph into an inevitable story after seeing the outcome, turning unknown paths into supposedly prior-known causes. Descriptive edges are not automatically causal or authorization edges; claims about effects and permission carry separate responsibilities.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Define each node completely as an object according to the task, including its identity criterion, boundaries, and identity; names or positions cannot substitute.

  2. 2

    State containment, jurisdiction, aggregation, membership overlap, propagation, resources, competition, and other relations by type.

  3. 3

    Allow multiple edges between the same endpoints, preserving each edge's direction, definition of the relation, and evidence.

  4. 4

    Identify common conditions; without grounds for a direct channel, add no direct edge, and explicitly mark unknowns.

  5. 5

    Give temporary channels clear start and end times, separate from long-term relations.

  6. 6

    Save pre-event and post-event snapshots, comparing change, preservation, and unresolved status node by node and edge by edge.

  7. 7

    Explain events only through relations covered by material; graph structure does not automatically generate causation, responsibility, or authorization.

Distinctions to keep clear

Single hierarchy tree

Can express one restricted vertical relation.

≠

Directed multirelational graph

Can retain multiple edge types, directions, overlaps, and temporary channels together.

Common condition

An external input relates to both ends simultaneously.

≠

Direct channel

Specified transmission between the two ends, requiring separate grounds.

Upper-level position

A position in a particular containment/jurisdiction/aggregation relation.

≠

More correct or more authorized

Epistemic and normative judgments that position cannot establish.

Temporary edge termination

One type of relation ceases to be open after its window.

≠

Object dissolution or overall transformation

Requires independent material on each node's identity criterion and other relations.

Different reverse-direction relations

Each direction has its own definition.

≠

Untyped bidirectional line

May obscure distinctions in content, direction, and responsibility.

Mathematical construction: a common input can create synchronization without a direct effectTeaching scenario

AssumptionsStipulated structural equations, no hidden additional channels, and intervention replacing only the A equation; no actual social or equipment data are involved.

Let common input E∈{0,1}, with targets A=E and B=2E. Natural observations are (A,B)=(0,0) or (1,2), perfectly synchronized. The model specifies only E→A and E→B, with no A→B. Holding E fixed and replacing A alone leaves B=2E. Synchronization therefore cannot itself support a direct edge.

BoundaryDoes not establish absence of real direct edges; their existence requires separate process evidence or proportionate comparisons.

Teaching construction: four nodes and seven edges, only three temporaryTeaching scenario

AssumptionsNodes, edges, and time are stipulated; containment edges represent membership structure, not causation/permission; condition edges hold by the stated assumptions.

A fictional component whole P contains components A and B, with two permanent containment edges. Common condition E connects separately to A and B, adding two condition edges. Only during [t₁,t₂), A→B opens separate information and supply edges, and B→A opens a request edge: three temporary relations. Within the window there are seven typed edges; outside it, closing those three leaves four long-term edges. If every node still satisfies its original identity criterion, channel closure cannot be recorded as dissolution of the whole P.

BoundaryNot a real component-operation diagram; no claim that actual material transfer, capacity, or authorization has been measured.

Teaching construction: precisely changing one edge after an eventTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll communication is constructed, change conditions are explicit, and no equipment configuration was implemented.

Suppose A-to-B information changes from one-way to allowing return information from B, while supplies remain only A→B and request-channel conditions are unchanged. Add or update the return-information edge with its time and evidence, without casually making the supply edge bidirectional too. A subsequent claim of effective feedback still requires checking whether the return updates A's later state; a new arrow alone is insufficient.

BoundaryCheck relationship updates, effective feedback, and permission changes separately.

Reporting lines and request paths in CAIB are different edgesDocumented case

CAIB F6.3-6 records the Debris Assessment Team reporting through MER to MMT; F6.3-7–8 separately discuss its imagery requests traveling through Johnson's engineering department. The focus here is separately representing the same team's organizational reporting relation and actual request path; a single organizational tree cannot reconstruct every information flow.

SourceCAIB Volume I, Chapter 6（2003）Printed p.171, F6.3-6–8Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsSupports only the two types of relation and path problems described in the report, not the complete network; node hierarchy is not directly interpreted as authorization or the sole cause.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTwo teams synchronize after the same external announcement, so a direct causal edge from team A to B is added.

What it limitsA common condition can explain synchronization; the direct channel requires separate evidence.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleAn A→B message edge and B→A request edge are merged into an untyped bidirectional arrow.

What it limitsThis loses relational content, direction, and respective conditions, preventing tracing of specific changes.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleTemporary collaboration ends, so every node and containment relation is relabeled dissolved.

What it limitsWhen only temporary-edge closure is established, retain the other relations; separately check node identity through the identity criterion.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleP is drawn at the top, so P's views must be more reliable and it may act upon every lower level.

What it limitsGraphic position generates neither epistemic priority nor permission within the scope of authorization.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Drawing a graph adds no empirical support; edges without material remain candidate/unknown, not filled in merely to make a connected picture.
  • A common-environment node does not rule out an additional real direct channel; the requirement is only not to add edges without evidence.
  • Containment edges are not automatically causal edges; jurisdiction edges also require valid authorization material, not just arrows.
  • Edges with different time windows cannot be silently combined into an eternally existing network.
  • After an event, change only nodes or edges demonstrated to have changed, preserving unchanged parts and unresolved points rather than rewriting the whole.

Scope and open questions

The same investigation separately describes reporting lines and request paths, making it suitable for illustrating why relationship types cannot be merged; the accompanying diagram is an independent fictional model and does not pretend to be NASA's actual complete organizational chart.

Why must two same-direction edges between the same endpoints still be separate?

Information and supplies can have different conditions, capacities, times, and evidence; they cannot substitute for one another.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

In the common-input example, does synchronization of A and B establish that A directly affects B?

No. Both are jointly determined by E; in the model, changing A while holding E fixed leaves B unchanged.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

How many edges are present inside and outside the window in the four-node example?

Inside: 2 containment + 2 common-condition + 3 temporary relations =7; outside: the 3 temporary edges close, leaving 4 long-term edges.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does the end of the window imply that P is no longer the original object?

No. Separately check whether P and every node still satisfy the identity criterion; ending a relation does not automatically change identity.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does adding information return from B to A already establish effective feedback?

Material showing that the return actually updates A's subsequent state is still needed; recording an arrow is only part of the relation layer.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Why cannot an upper level directly mean greater authority?

Here it indicates only a position in a particular relation; power must be established by specific valid authorization material.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above
